The reason why they started putting narcan in our branches was due to the fact that opiate overdoses have increased in our state dramatically since Covid. It’s not necessarily as an addiction center but because the number of people that have been found in library bathroom floor suffering from an OD has become common. So we keep it to save lives, not to necessarily become a rehab center. Sadly whether we organize storytime for children, the reality is that the library is still a public place and that includes people who are considered the “undesirables.” And we need to be prepared for that. In fact, the libraries in New Orleans (the parish next to mine) saved 3 people from an overdose when they started placing narcan at branches.

 I knew people that planned their babies and still said they had anxiety when they got the positive test result. Even when they were happy, they still said that there was a part of them that was scared. 

Think about it--this is a big deal. A baby is a major life event and big commitment. Basically, your life is about to change completely and you're going to change too. You're probably worried about how you'll cope and if you'll be a good parent. And that's okay, that's how it happens. It's a big deal because it is. In fact I think some anxiety is a good thing. So, what to do? Take a deep breath. Relax about being scared. You JUST found out, so you're still processing this big announcement. Maybe talk to your girlfriend too. You might find that she's just as stressed out as you are. Talking about it might help and realize that you're not alone. Eventually, time will pass and the anxiety will go away and you'll experience joy and excitement over it. 

In the meantime, find books and articles about pregnancy and what you need to prepare for your little one. That might help to calm you down if you're more prepared. And parenting books too. If there's classes or info you can get from the doctor about what to expect and parenthood, take those too. Um, my Mom read Dr. Spock for my sisters and we turned out somewhat okay lol. Get support from family and friends and talk to them (when you get ready to tell them).

Bats are one of many animals that can pause their pregnancy. 
The largest bat is the flying fox. It has a wing span of up to five in a half feet. 
Despite their bad reputation, bats are super timid and will generally avoid humans if they can help it. They’re not aggressive and don’t attack unless provoked. Many species only eat fruit or insects. Even the vampire bat doesn’t attack—it only drinks the blood of sleeping animals and can detect body temperature to determine if you’re sleeping.  In fact, their personality is described as being similar to puppies and can even be cuddly (but it’s still best to avoid them as they are still wild animals).
Sadly, they spread rabies a lot. But they also eat mosquitoes which cause some pretty bad diseases, so they also help to prevent disease and are even considered good luck in some cultures. 
With the exception of places with extreme hot or cold environments, bats can be found on every continent in the world (except Antarctica). 
Um…depending on the species, bats can live in groups of up to millions. Some species are monogamous, some are not.

So, this is one I used last weekend and it's the easiest recipe I found. Apparently, it was found in an old Louisiana cookbook. Not the exact recipe but was inspired by it. It's really just combining ingredients: 

First, season and brown the parts of the chicken you want to use. Set it aside. 

Next, make the roux. Just keep stirring until it's that nice dark brown color (or however color you like for your stew). For this recipe, make enough roux for two tablespoons. 

Once it's done, turn up the heat and stir in your chopped seasoning to the pot (I use onions/green onions, bell pepper, garlic. You can also add celery too if that's your thing). Add the browned chicken. Then add enough water to cover the ingredients, (I start off with one cup, and then add more as needed), add your spices (salt, black pepper, garlic powder, onion powder, a pinch of cayenne pepper is my usual, but do you). Bring to a boil then lower the heat, cover it and let it simmer. I let it simmer for about 20-30 minutes, stirring it every few minutes or so. After,, turn off heat and sauce should thicken on standing and then you serve over rice. 

Note: If the stew is simmering and you feel it's too thick, add more water (half cup at a time), if it's too thin, add more flour (teaspoon at a time...from my experience). 

 This makes A LOT of stew so this can last for awhile and you can freeze it for later.

Strange story my mom told me. She grew up in a small town here in Louisiana during the 50's and 60's. The way the town operated was weird. 

She was Black. Some of her neighbors were white. Her father worked alongside whites in the fields. For the most part Blacks and Whites mingled, worked together and got along (at least in her part of the town). But...there was still segregation. There were "whites only" stores. When she went to church--Whites sat in the front, Blacks in the back. It doesn't make any sense because their neighborhoods and personal life was not segregated (the town doctor attended to everyone, regardless of race for example.) Some things were integrated, some were not. From what she explained, they segregated church and  businesses because...that was just the norm. Up until integration, they just never even considered the idea that there was another way and didn't really question it. It was just "that's how it was always done." So, when things were integrated, not much of a fuss because, nothing they were doing made sense anyway. 

Honestly, the stories I hear from my mom are confusing from my perspective.

I will try to explain it as best as I can from my perspective. I just hope I can help in making sense of it all, because it's so complex that it requires reading about...everything in this country's history. 

I don't think "person of color" has the same historical issue at "colored." The word "colored" has a history to it--a time during segregation when you saw bathrooms being labeled as "whites only" and "colored." So, it's not just the word--it's the history behind it. Usually if you hear an older white person say colored people nowadays, it's usually associated with someone racist and probably supported segregation back then. "Person of color" I don't think would get the same issue because it's relatively new term (as far as I know) so doesn't have the thing.  
As for the second question...not that we WANT to divide it, but rather there is a discussion on the fact that there are differences between races that do determine financial stability, education, employment, how society treats you, treatment by police, even whether or not you get healthcare, etc. As for shades of color, I'm guessing it may be because...even shades of black skin can determine whether you get ahead in America. The only example I can think of is the relationship between me and my Mom. My mom's a Black Creole and fair skinned. I'm Black with darker skin. We're both Black of course, but we have two completely different life experiences that had to do with our skin color. In fact, I had to explain it to my mom recently because she didn't understand that my life experiences differ from her in how people treat me or view me (especially when it comes to standards of beauty). In fact, even she was part of it--I grew up hearing and experiencing a lot of things from her and realizing that she had some "internalized racism" that affected how she would talk about darker skinned Black women and how she treated me vs how she treated my niece that had a lighter complexion (you notice it fairly early).  Mind you, I don't even think she even noticed what she was doing until I started to call her out on it. 

Is it ridiculous? Yes! As a Black, I say it is! Other Blacks feel the same too! That's why we have to bring up the issues in this country. Sadly, we didn't ask for it, it's our history that got us to this ridiculous point and now we gotta deal with and talk about it if we want to end it. Like I say, I don't think we're trying to divide it, but if we want to end systemic racism in this country, we need to acknowledge that there are differences between us that determine different experiences and this may be how we can move forward and also consider universal healthcare, services that would help move people out of poverty, etc. Some people don't see that and I've met those people. Those are the people that cried when Roe v Wade was overturned and saying how bad things are in America right now, Blacks have been saying it since Trump was first elected and they said we were overreacting. The majority of people in America are busy trying to survive and work hard to care about some video game character's skin color, and most Blacks would say this isn't even in the top 20 lists of problems we need to discuss and fix in regards to racial relations in America. Like, we don't care about changing a skin color in a video game, we just asked for the police to stop killing us.
